author: Al Jazeera English
description:
The Caribbean is facing a growing sargassum seaweed crisis, with huge quantities washing onto beaches across the region and threatening tourism, ecosystems and public health.

Mexico’s Riviera Maya has been particularly affected, with the influx reaching thousands of tonnes of seaweed each day.

As the algae decomposes on beaches, it can release toxic gases, raising health concerns for residents and tourists. Scientists also warn that the accumulation of sargassum can damage seagrass ecosystems and affect beach stability.

The crisis is putting pressure on Mexico’s tourism industry, while the Mexican Navy has stepped up efforts to collect the seaweed before it reaches the shore.

But some businesses are looking at sargassum differently.

Companies including Carbonwave and Sargablock are developing ways to transform the invasive algae into products such as bio-fertilizers, footwear and construction materials.

Could an environmental crisis become a new source of sustainable materials?
title: Mexico’s Caribbean beaches overwhelmed by record sargassum influx I Inside Latin America

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
The Ig Nobel Prizes, the satirical awards that celebrate the quirky side of science, were held outside the US for the first time this year due to travel concerns. Researchers from around the world, many in costume, travelled to collect their awards from actual Nobel laureates, for research ranging from cockroaches worn on heads to nose-blowing, kissing cavemen and buried underwear.

Social psychologist Paul Piff's team won for finding that wealth makes people more self-interested, entitled and greedy, after discovering that rich people took twice as much candy from a bowl meant for children. Another team was honoured for solving the problem of splash-back from urinals, proving that even the strangest questions can lead to useful answers.

Nobel economics laureate Esther Duflo, who helped present the awards, said the point of the ceremony is science that makes people laugh first, and think afterwards. As these researchers show, sometimes the silliest ideas turn out to be the brightest.
title: Ig Nobel Prizes showcase surprising science

description:
Nepal's government says the severe flooding is not just a humanitarian crisis but an economic one, with hydropower plants, roads, bridges and entire villages damaged or destroyed. Authorities estimate that rebuilding could cost $5 billion, and with thousands of people, many of them breadwinners, still missing, the economic toll continues to rise.

Chirachit Kurki, whose aunt and cousin were swept away while waiting to cross the Nepal-China border, says the disaster is not simply natural but the result of global warming caused by humans. Twelve hydroelectric plants in the Trishuli Basin, developed with help from China and international lenders, are now severely damaged, and tens of thousands of families need new homes.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
As the scale of Nepal's flood disaster becomes clearer, attention is turning to who will pay for the damage. Nearly all of Nepal's electricity comes from hydropower, generated at more than 200 facilities. At least 12 of them, spread across two river basins, were damaged in the floods, wiping out more than 10 percent of the country's generation capacity and affecting both domestic supply and the roughly $200 million a year Nepal earns from electricity exports.

The glaciers that once gave Nepal its hydropower advantage are becoming a growing liability, as high-altitude regions of the Himalayas warm nearly 50 percent faster than the global average. Nepal accounts for just 0.1 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet is paying a disproportionately heavy price, while China, the US and India remain the world's largest emitters.

Al Jazeera's Julide Ayger reports.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Togo has secured overwhelming support at the United Nations for a resolution promoting more geographically accurate world maps, challenging the widely used Mercator projection.

The Mercator projection makes areas closer to the poles appear much larger while distorting the relative size of Africa and other regions.

Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey says distorted maps can reinforce inaccurate perceptions across generations. The government plans to introduce new maps in schools by the end of the year.

The resolution passed despite opposition from the United States, which criticised the initiative as an “ideological agenda”. Russia backed the move, describing it as a victory for African unity and a challenge to historical injustice.

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Mail-in voting has become the centre of an intensifying legal and political battle in the United States ahead of the midterm elections.

President Donald Trump has repeatedly opposed mail-in ballots, raising concerns about election security. Democrats and voting rights advocates argue that restrictions could suppress participation and make it harder for eligible voters to cast their ballots.

A series of legal challenges has produced conflicting rulings, with some voting restrictions blocked by courts before being reinstated on appeal.

Meanwhile, states including North Carolina have already begun sending ballots to voters, adding urgency to the legal disputes.

The US Postal Service is also facing questions over whether it is prepared to handle the volume of election mail and meet new technology and processing requirements.

With the midterms approaching, the fight over mail-in voting could have major implications for how millions of Americans cast their ballots.

Al Jazeera’s Eva Mc
title: US mail-in voting rules face legal battle ahead of midterm elections

author: Al Jazeera English
description:
Cuba is introducing major economic reforms as the country struggles with severe fuel and electricity shortages and a deepening economic crisis.

The government is opening parts of the tourism sector to private foreign capital and allowing Cubans living abroad to own businesses, in an effort to attract investment and generate much-needed revenue.

But the reforms come as Cuba faces persistent power outages, fuel shortages and scarcity of basic goods. Residents across the island continue to deal with daily blackouts and worsening economic hardship.

Cuban officials acknowledge the difficult environment for foreign investment, particularly in the energy sector. Economists say the reforms are overdue but question whether they will be enough to reverse the country's economic decline without broader political changes.

At the same time, the United States has announced new sanctions against Cuba, adding further pressure to an economy already struggling to recover.

Al Jazeera’s Julia Galiano
title: Cuba unveils economic reforms as energy crisis deepens under US sanctions

The allegations come as Reform UK expands its political influence and faces increasing scrutiny over how it operates and is funded.

At the party’s conference in Birmingham, supporters expressed mixed views, with some remaining loyal to Farage while others voiced distrust of political leaders.

The controversy highlights the challenges facing Reform UK as it moves further into Britain’s political establishment.
